summary.title: What Every Programmer Should Know About SSDs
summary.one_liner: You learn why NAND flash SSDs behave differently from spinning disks (parallel flash chips, asymmetric read/write latency, out-of-place writes, garbage collection, write amplification, overprovisioning) and how to exploit them.
takeaways: SSD random reads take about 100us versus about 10ms for a random disk access, and SSD writes are cached in RAM so their visible latency is lower than the actual flash write latency of about 1ms.
Flash SSDs reach high bandwidth by issuing many concurrent IO requests (via many threads or asynchronous interfaces like libaio or io_uring) to keep all flash chips busy.
NAND pages cannot be overwritten in place; updates go to new locations tracked by a flash translation layer mapping table, and garbage collection erases blocks later.

Write amplification is the ratio of physical to logical writes; worst-case is 1/(1-f) for fill factor f, so random writes on a nearly full SSD are very costly, which is why overprovisioning of about 10-20% helps.
summary.summary: The article explains how flash-based SSDs differ from magnetic disks from a programmer's point of view. It covers latency and parallelism, the asymmetry between cached writes and actual NAND write latency, and why out-of-place writes require a flash translation layer and garbage collection. It uses a toy example with erase blocks and pages to illustrate these mechanisms, then gives a table of worst-case write amplification by fill factor. It closes with hardware figures for a Samsung server SSD and pointers to further reading, including a CIDR 2020 paper on the Linux I/O stack.
